body:
Jainism and its early community

Jainism developed as an important religious tradition in northern India during the period when new kingdoms, towns and religious ideas were emerging. According to Jain tradition, Mahavira was the 24th Tirthankara. A Tirthankara is a spiritual teacher who shows the path to liberation.

Mahavira lived in the 6th century BCE. His teachings emphasised ahimsa, or non-injury to living beings, together with truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy and non-possession. These principles encouraged disciplined living and the reduction of attachment to worldly possessions.

The Jain community included monks, nuns and lay followers. Monks and nuns renounced ordinary household life and followed strict rules of conduct. Lay followers continued to live in society while supporting the religious community and observing Jain principles according to their circumstances.

How support helped Jainism spread

The spread of Jainism depended on more than the teachings of individual religious leaders. Travelling monks, lay followers, merchants, rulers and ministers all contributed in different ways.

Merchants and lay followers

Jainism received substantial support from trading communities. Merchants and other householders provided food, shelter and resources to ascetics. This support allowed religious teachers to continue their journeys and helped Jain communities become established in towns.

Strict observance of ahimsa could be especially difficult in occupations involving unavoidable injury to living beings. For example, cultivation sometimes required farmers to destroy insects to protect crops. This helps explain why merchants became prominent supporters, although it does not mean that all merchants were Jains or that farmers could not follow Jainism.

Rulers and ministers

Royal patronage could provide resources for religious establishments and encourage the construction or maintenance of places used by Jain communities. Ministers and wealthy private donors also supported religious buildings. Royal patronage, however, does not automatically prove that every supporting ruler personally adopted Jainism.

Expansion to different regions

Over several centuries, Jainism spread from its early centres in northern India to other regions, notably Gujarat, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. Monastic travel transmitted teachings, while local followers and donors helped establish lasting religious institutions.

Two regions became particularly significant. Karnataka developed important Jain monastic and pilgrimage centres, including Shravanabelagola. Gujarat became a major centre of Jain learning, manuscript preservation, royal patronage and pilgrimage.

The spread of Jainism was a gradual historical process. A traditional account linking a famous ruler to a region is not, by itself, proof that the ruler introduced Jainism there for the first time.

Prelims focus

  • Mahavira is regarded as the 24th Tirthankara of Jainism.
  • Ahimsa is a central principle of Jain teaching.
  • Merchants were important lay supporters of Jain monks and nuns.
  • Jainism spread over centuries to Gujarat, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
  • Trap: The spread of Jainism cannot be attributed to royal patronage alone.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, chapter 7, New Questions and Ideas, printed pp. 69–71, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, theme 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, printed pp. 88–89.]

title: How Jainism Spread Beyond Its Early Centres

body:
The Mauryan period and Jain traditions

The Mauryan dynasty emerged as a major political power in northern India in the late 4th century BCE. Chandragupta Maurya established Mauryan rule around 321 BCE. Jain traditions associate him with the religious teacher Bhadrabahu and with the southward movement of Jain ascetics.

These accounts are important for understanding the traditional history of Jainism in Karnataka. They must, however, be distinguished from events independently established through contemporary evidence.

Chandragupta Maurya and Bhadrabahu

According to a later Digambara Jain tradition, a prolonged famine occurred in Magadha. The Jain teacher Bhadrabahu led a group of ascetics southward to escape its effects. Chandragupta Maurya is said to have renounced his throne, accompanied the group and adopted an ascetic life.

The tradition connects Bhadrabahu and Chandragupta with Shravanabelagola in present-day Karnataka, where they are believed to have practised severe austerities and ended their lives through religious fasting.

The Svetambara tradition gives a different account of Bhadrabahu's movements, associating him with Nepal rather than the same southward migration. Therefore, the migration of Chandragupta and Bhadrabahu should be described as a traditional association, not an undisputed historical fact.

Chandragupta Maurya and Karnataka: The important association is with Bhadrabahu, renunciation and Shravanabelagola. This is different from the later construction of the famous Bahubali statue at the same pilgrimage centre.

Samprati: the Mauryan patron of Jainism

Samprati, a grandson of Ashoka, is remembered in Jain tradition as an important royal patron during the 3rd century BCE. Svetambara accounts particularly associate him with the Jain teacher Suhastin, also called Suhastisuri, whom he is said to have encountered at Ujjain.

According to these traditions, Samprati supported Jain religious activities, encouraged the movement of monks and promoted the establishment or maintenance of Jain temples and images. The accounts connect his patronage with the wider spread of Jainism, including western India.

These descriptions come largely from later Jain literature. The exact scale of Samprati's building activities and the geographical extent of his religious initiatives cannot be treated as independently verified facts.

Distinguishing 3 Mauryan figures

Chandragupta Maurya is traditionally linked with Jain renunciation and the journey south. Ashoka is especially associated with the promotion of Buddhism. Samprati is celebrated in Jain tradition for supporting Jain religious institutions and the movement of teachers.

Prelims focus

  • Chandragupta Maurya established Mauryan rule around 321 BCE.
  • Digambara tradition associates Chandragupta with Bhadrabahu and Shravanabelagola.
  • Shravanabelagola is in Karnataka.
  • Samprati was Ashoka's grandson and is remembered as a Jain patron.
  • Suhastin is traditionally associated with Samprati at Ujjain.
  • Trap: Chandragupta's journey south is a Jain traditional account, not an undisputed historical event.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, chapter 8, Ashoka, the Emperor Who Gave Up War, and the chronology of ancient India; Nalini Balbir, Jainpedia, Sacred writings, section Crises and losses, consulted 18 November 2026; Nikita Mohta, Ashoka helped spread Buddhism far and wide. How his grandson did the same for Jainism, The Indian Express, 1 April 2026, consulted 18 November 2026; Karnataka Tourism, Shravanabelagola, consulted 18 November 2026.]

body:
Kharavela: a ruler associated with Jainism

Kharavela was an ancient ruler of Kalinga, a region in eastern India associated principally with present-day Odisha. He belonged to the Mahameghavahana, or Chedi, ruling line.

Kharavela is generally placed in the later centuries BCE, commonly around the 1st century BCE, although his precise dating is debated. For preliminary study, his association with Kalinga, Jainism and the caves near Bhubaneswar is more secure than a single exact regnal date.

Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves

The Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves are situated in neighbouring hills near Bhubaneswar, Odisha. They are especially important for understanding Jain religious activity and royal support in ancient Kalinga.

The caves include spaces used by Jain ascetics. Royal patronage made it possible to provide places where monks could stay and practise religious discipline, including during periods when travel was difficult.

Kharavela and members of his royal circle are associated with the creation or support of caves and facilities for Jain ascetics. This illustrates a direct form of patronage: providing resources and accommodation to a religious community.

The Hathigumpha inscription

The best-known inscription associated with Kharavela is the Hathigumpha inscription, located on Udayagiri Hill. Hathigumpha means Elephant Cave.

The inscription is written in Prakrit using the Brahmi script. It records matters connected with Kharavela's reign and reflects his association with Jain religious traditions, including references to Jain spiritual figures and support for ascetics.

The distinction between the inscription and the cave complex is important. Hathigumpha is on Udayagiri, while Udayagiri and Khandagiri together form the well-known group of Jain caves.

Kharavela and Ashoka were different rulers

Ashoka's conquest of Kalinga took place during the Mauryan period in the 3rd century BCE. Kharavela ruled Kalinga later. They should not be treated as the same ruler or as contemporaries in the Kalinga War.

Their religious associations also differ. Ashoka is especially associated with Buddhism, while Kharavela is an important example of a ruler associated with Jainism.

Prelims focus

  • Kharavela was a ruler of Kalinga, associated with present-day Odisha.
  • He belonged to the Mahameghavahana or Chedi ruling line.
  • Udayagiri and Khandagiri are near Bhubaneswar.
  • The Hathigumpha inscription is on Udayagiri Hill.
  • Hathigumpha is associated with Kharavela and Jainism.
  • Trap: Kharavela was not the Mauryan emperor who fought the Kalinga War; that emperor was Ashoka.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, chapter 4, Post-Mauryan Trends in Indian Art and Architecture, printed p. 45; e-PG Pathshala, Indian Epigraphy, module 28, Hathigumpha Inscription of Kharavela, sections on Kharavela's religious patronage and the inscription, consulted 18 November 2026; Government of Odisha, Odisha Tourism, Udayagiri and Khandagiri Caves, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Jain ascetics quietly walk and rest beside simple rock-cut caves in the wooded hills of Udayagiri and Khandagiri.
pictures.caption: Rock-cut caves near Bhubaneswar provided spaces for Jain ascetics.

title: Kharavela and the Royal Patronage of Jainism in Kalinga

body:
Why Jain councils were held

Mahavira's teachings were initially passed from teachers to disciples through oral transmission. Successive generations of Jain monks preserved and recited religious teachings rather than relying on a single written book.

Over time, the Jain community became concerned that some teachings might be forgotten, altered or lost. The movement of monks across different regions and disruptions such as famine made the preservation of oral traditions more difficult.

Religious teachers therefore organised formal recitations or councils, known in Jain tradition as vachanas. At these gatherings, learned monks brought together teachings known to different groups and attempted to preserve an accepted collection.

A Jain council was an assembly or formal recitation intended to collect, preserve or organise Jain religious teachings. It was not an assembly of political representatives.

Important councils and their associations

Place and approximate periodAssociated teacherMain significance
Pataliputra, traditionally placed in the early Mauryan periodSthulabhadraEarly recitation and collection of orally transmitted teachings
Mathura, around the 4th century CESkandilaRecitation of Jain teachings in northern India
Valabhi, around the 4th century CENagarjunaAnother recitation, associated with a different textual tradition
Valabhi, around the 5th to early 6th century CEDevardhigani KshamashramanaFinal major redaction and writing down of the surviving Svetambara scriptures

The exact dates assigned to the councils are uncertain. Their traditional accounts were recorded after the events they describe. The important distinction is between the earlier recitations and the later Valabhi redaction, which is particularly associated with the preservation of the Svetambara canon in written form.

Valabhi: the Gujarat connection

Valabhi, also written Vallabhi, was an important centre in the Saurashtra region of present-day Gujarat. It became closely associated with the collection and written preservation of Jain religious texts.

The final major Valabhi council is associated with Devardhigani Kshamashramana, also called Devavachaka. The surviving teachings recognised by the Svetambara tradition were collected and put into written form so that further losses could be reduced.

References give different dates for this redaction. Some traditional reckonings place it around 453 or 466 CE, while other accounts place it in the early 6th century CE. Therefore, an exact year should not be presented as universally settled.

Did all Jain traditions accept the same scriptures?

No. The 2 major Jain traditions, Svetambara and Digambara, differ over the preservation and authority of the earliest scriptures.

The Valabhi collection is particularly important to the Svetambara tradition. Digambara Jains do not accept that collection as an authentic preservation of the complete original canon and recognise a different body of authoritative writings.

Consequently, it is inaccurate to say that the Valabhi council produced a scripture collection accepted without disagreement by every Jain sect. It is also important not to confuse these Jain assemblies with the Buddhist councils, which concerned the preservation of Buddhist teachings.

Prelims focus

  • Pataliputra is traditionally associated with Sthulabhadra.
  • Mathura is associated with Skandila.
  • An earlier Valabhi recitation is associated with Nagarjuna.
  • The final major Valabhi redaction is associated with Devardhigani Kshamashramana.
  • Valabhi is in Gujarat and is important for the Svetambara Agamas.
  • Trap: The Valabhi redaction was not accepted as the authoritative canon by all Jain traditions.

[Sources: Nalini Balbir, Jainpedia, Sacred writings, sections Chain of oral transmission, Crises and losses and Svetambara canon, consulted 18 November 2026; Jainpedia, Devarddhi-gani, section on the recitation councils, consulted 18 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, chapter 7, New Questions and Ideas, printed p. 70, and the volume's ancient-history chronology.]
